balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For China Merchants Securities Co., Ltd.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For China Merchants Securities Co., Ltd.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For China Merchants Securities Co., Ltd.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For China Merchants Securities Co., Ltd.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For China Merchants Securities Co., Ltd.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For China Merchants Securities Co., Ltd.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For China Merchants Securities Co., Ltd.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For China Merchants Securities Co., Ltd.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For China Merchants Securities Co., Ltd.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

revenueMix.title: Revenue composition: fees vs. investment gains
revenueMix.content:
CMSC's income statement blends three economically different streams: fee & commission income (brokerage, underwriting, asset/fund management -- stable, tied to client activity), interest income (margin financing, repo, treasury -- stable, tied to the loan book) and net investment gains (proprietary trading/FICC/derivatives/alternative investment -- highly volatile, correlated with A-share/H-share direction). Only the first two are shown against CSV columns that exist; interest income is not separately broken out in the exported data.

For China Merchants Securities Co., Ltd.: H1 FY2026 net profit roughly doubled YoY (+104.9%), but net investment gains rose 213% to RMB12.9bn (47% of revenue) on the STAR 50/ChiNext rally, while fee & commission income grew far more modestly. The headline growth is overwhelmingly a market-beta story, not a client-franchise story.

What to watch:

  • Net investment income reversing sharply when the equity rally cools -- it swings both ways
  • Fee & commission income as the more durable, repeatable base of earnings
  • Log scale needed here: investment gains can approach zero or even turn negative in a down market, so treat a flat or dipping bar as the expected cyclical pattern, not an anomaly

balanceScale.title: Margin lending book and customer balances
balanceScale.content:
Margin accounts receivable is the margin financing and securities lending loan book -- client borrowing secured against their portfolios. Customer balances is client money held on account (cash held in trust, not CMSC's own asset, but part of the operating scale of the brokerage).

For China Merchants Securities Co., Ltd.: both lines are scale indicators for the wealth-management/brokerage franchise rather than profitability measures -- margin book growth drives interest income, and customer balances approximate the breadth of the ~22 million client-account base. Growth here does not by itself mean rising profit, since both carry collateral/counterparty risk in a market downturn.

What to watch:

  • Margin book growing faster than the broader market (concentration/leverage risk building)
  • Customer balances stalling while investment gains rise (a sign the profit surge is proprietary-book-driven, not client-driven)
